To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the diversity of echinoderms in the Caribbean region has been significantly underestimated in previous studies due to taphonomy and collection bias, (2) echinoderms are a key component of the Caribbean fauna, with the most common living groups having been represented throughout the Cenzoic and (3) the Caribbean echinoderm fauna was strongly affected by the Eocene– Oligocene extinctions, with the roots (at least at the generic) of the extant
the echinoderm fauna of the Caribbean has changed through time in a manner similar to the rest of the region's fauna, but that echinoderms have been under-collected and under-studied.

the Caribbean echinoderma have a rich fossil record that has been under-exploited and that this record indicates that the modern faunas of Caribbean echinoids and crinoids are at least as old as the Oligocene, and that the modern asteroid and ophiuroid faunas of the region are much younger.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a better understanding of the diversity and distribution of Caribbean fossil echinoderans through time and space, with a view to improving the quality of palaeoecological and palaeobiogeographical reconstructions.
the application of the principles of palaeontology to the reconstruction of the history of the Caribbean biota during the Cenzoic.

the application of a more holistic approach to the study of the Cenozoicoceanography and biogeography of the Caribbean region, which is leading to a more consistent and balanced picture of the evolution of its echinoderms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there has been a remarkable stability in the diversity of echinoderms in the Antillean area throughout the Cenozoi
echinoids were the most diverse group in the Caribbean during the Cenzoic, with the other groups being of comparable importance.
there is no evidence for significant faunal change in the echinoderma of the region from the Eocene to the present.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Caribbean region was not as depauperate in its echinoderm fauna as has been commonly thought.

the modern Caribbean echinoderm fauna was in existence by the early Oligocene, but that the modern composition and diversity of the fauna is the result of a long period of faunal change that has been obscured by the focus on complete tests in previous studies.
the modern echinoderm assemblage of the Caribbean region is a product of the Oligocene–Pleistocene.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diversity of echinoderms in the Caribbean during the Cenozic was much greater than previously recognized.

, while it may not be possible to reconstruct the diversity of the Caribbean echinoderma fauna at any given point in the past with the same precision that is possible for the modern fauna, it is clear that the fossil record is sufficiently complete that the major changes in faunal composition that have occurred since the Eocene can be reconstructed with confidence.

the Caribbean region is not a ‘living museum’ for echinoderms, as it is for many other taxa (e.g. corals, molluscs, sponges, foraminiferans, etc.), and that the fossil record is essential for understanding the evolutionary history of echinoderms in the region.
